newsitem.title: VENEZUELA: Venezuela oil chief calls for end to OPEC quotas.
newsitem.headline: Venezuela oil chief calls for end to OPEC quotas.

text.p: Luis Giusti, head of Venezuela's state-owned oil company Petroleos de Venezuela, called Friday for the Organization of Petroleum Exporting Countries (OPEC) to drop its system of restricting output in favor of increasing market share.

Speaking to journalists in Venezuela's Miraflores presidential palace, he said Venezuela had initiated a debate in the 11-member cartel about its future and he saw a bleak future without structural change.

"We have to ask ourselves who benefits (from the quota system)," he said. "If prices rise, (OPEC) producers see some benefit from the price, but this is compensated by a reduction in volume. The real beneficiary from price rises is non-OPEC and, even worse for us, they take every percent share of the market that (OPEC) shuts in."

OPEC ministers are due to meet in 10 days' time to decide on a new production ceiling and make their usual calls for quota compliance. Venezuela's Energy and Mines Minister has already endorsed other countries' calls for no change in the group's 25 million barrels per day (bpd) ceiling, even while actual production runs at 27 million bpd.

Venezuela, one of OPEC's founder members, has long pursued a policy of expanding oil output while agreeing to unchanged official quotas at OPEC meetings. It now has the unenviable title as OPEC's biggest quota violator with production running at 3.2 million bpd, against its official limit of 2.4 million.

"Thanks to an initiative of the Venezuelan government, OPEC is thinking about its current and future role," Giusti said. "If we continue with a narrow thinking about quotas, we, as an institution, have a very dark future."

Asked whether OPEC dropping the quota system would lead to a price drop, Giusti said there was a "floor" to oil prices at about $14-15 per barrel of North Sea Brent crude. He said this floor was formed partly by extra demand for oil at lower prices, and partly by the United States oil industry which had a major interest in maintaining profitability.
